newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia scepticism over reported purge on gangsters.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia scepticism over reported purge on gangsters.

text.p: Western diplomats and Bosnian Moslems said on Thursday they were deeply sceptical about reports of a possible crackdown against the Croat nationalist mafia that dominates the divided town of Mostar.

Croatian media reports that the most powerful warlord in Croat-held western Mostar, Mladen Naletilic, had been arrested this week set off speculation a purge was under way against politically-connected Croat gangsters.
Authorities offered few details of the Naletilic case and the other reported arrests in western Mostar. Local Bosnian Croat media made no mention of any crackdown.
"We fear this is another bluff," said Senad Efica, a journalist in Moslem-controlled eastern Mostar.
Western envoys said they suspected the Croatian government might be trying to give the appearance of a purge against its proteges, who have been blamed for violent attacks in Mostar this month.
"This is just cosmetic," said one Western official, who asked not to be named.
"There will be no genuine crackdown because the international community has no political will to take care of this problem."
Croat gangsters running western Mostar enjoy strong links to Croatia's powerful Defence Minister Gojko Susak, who backed their efforts to carve out a separate Croat statelet during the Bosnian war.
Bosnian Moslem leaders have repeatedly called on the United States and European powers to force Croatian President Franjo Tudjman to remove his proteges, who have blocked efforts to reunify Mostar.
Croat gansters rose to prominence during a vicious Moslem-Croat war in 1994 that destroyed much of the town and left it divided between the rival communities.

Tensions flared this month in Mostar after armed Croats, including policemen, opened fire on a group of Moslems trying to visit a cemetery in the Croat-held western sector. One Moslem man was killed and at least 20 people were wounded.

International police investigators issued a report this week which clearly pinned blame for the violence on Croat police. The investigators concluded that the policemen had resorted to lethal force without justification.

Croat leaders in Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation have refused to endorse the results of the investigation and have yet to arrest any of the police who were photographed shooting at retreating Moslem marchers.
The Moslem deputy mayor of Mostar, Safet Orucevic, said he was waiting for firm evidence that hardliners in western Mostar had been removed once and for all.
"It is not enough to state something. They have to show if the arrests really occurred", he told Reuters.
The Mostar situation was threatening to destroy the Moslem-Croat federation and the Dayton peace agreement, he said.

"If we want the federation to go forward, then we have to clean this wound of Mostar completely... If not, if we say there is no will for co-existence, then we are diagnosing the Dayton peace agreement as dead."
Orucevic said although he was sceptical about the reported crackdown, the Mostar gangsters would become a political liability for Tudjman among Croatian voters who dislike Bosnian Croat hardliners.
He urged major powers to threaten Tudjman's government with political or economic sanctions.
"The time for pretty words has passed. There must be decisive pressure on the political authorities in Croatia," said Orucevic.
